title: Research Taste in History
author: Benjamin Breen
summary: Breen asks how history education will change under AI and answers that eccentricity and creativity will matter more, since language models are strong at memorization and feedback but stuck in a median perspective. He recalls his Oxford tutor Allan Chapman, who made him learn Sumerian-Babylonian mathematics for no obvious payoff. The central argument is that apparently useless knowledge and alien epistemologies are the foundation of research taste in history. The move is to argue for teaching the history of science through its wrong turns rather than as a chain of triumphs. He concludes that the real value lay in being asked to live inside another system of thought.
points: AI excels at drill and brute-force research but gravitates to a median, bland perspective.
A tutor's demand to learn Sumerian math taught how to think rather than what to know.
Teaching only triumphant discoveries hides the wrong turns that explain them.
Useless knowledge is presented as the basis of research taste.
Algorithmic culture flattens thought, so people who inhabit alien worldviews grow more valuable.
quotes: Yet they remain stuck in a median perspective, a sort of averaged-out, clichéd intellectual blandness that helps explain why frontier models still lack “research taste” in humanistic disciplines.

If you teach the history of science, medicine, and technology only as a series of triumphant discoveries, you fail to capture the thought processes that actually led to those discoveries — and the thousand other wrong turns and odd byways that coexisted and competed with them.
In other words, useless knowledge is not useless at all. It is, in fact, the foundation of developing research taste in history.

A system optimized for writing clean code or for providing helpful answers may in fact prove distinctly unhelpful when tasked with finding something new in fields, like history, which cannot provide immediate feedback about whether an idea is promising or not.
Before Chapman, I had been told that other number systems and other cosmologies existed. But I had never been asked to actually try to live inside them.
